AN APPRECIATION
Mr. Victor G, Bareh is one of the few Khasi writers who
took pains — to bring back to life, certain personalities
of undated Khasi history. One of such writings is the drama
'U Tirot Singh which has since been translated into English.
Others of his writings sre based on legends and traditions,
yet through diligence and painstaking efforts he has produced
for the benefit of the reading public in these hills. I shall at
present confine my appreciation of "U Tirot Singh" only.
'U Tirot Singh" gives a vivid picture of the spirit and
determination of Tirot Singh, the Syiem of Nongkhiaw, when
the British came to these hills. The drama depicts the events
leading ftom a friendly relationship of the Khasis with the
Ca -t India Company, to the anti British struggle put up by U

Tirot Singh Syiem, and his contemporary, U Bor Manick.
Sy em of the composite state of Shillong (the present Khyrim and
Mylliem) Syiemships. The Khasi hills were then covered with
thick forests and not barren es they are now ; therefore the
puerlla warfare was adopted by the Khasi warriors The
British, though with superrior arms and equpment, found it
not ico easy to subdue the Khasi Chiefs through difficult
terrains of the hills. The virility ard stamina of the Khasi
warriors of those days put the Brifish to heavy strain in men
end money. Ultimately the Khasi Syiems had to be accepted
as friends and allif s through treaties and engagements entered
between them and the Brit ! sh, which, as one Viceroy remarked
that brave enemies make good friends
Of the minor characters introduced in the Drama was U
Bor Manick Syiem of Khyrim and Mylliem, who joined hands with
U Tirot Singh wi h a bid to drive the British out of these hills.
While U Tirot Singh was concentrating his fight on the Borduar
side, U Bor Manick put up a fierce fight in the Beitoila
(Spelt Bortula in the Drama) area. This area is not far from the
Umthna river where Nongkhiaw now meets Mylliem. It appears
that U Bor Manick's warriors did use firearms besides the tradi

tional spear end shield, and bows and arrows. The remnants of
these aims were picked up from Lyngkyrdem and also found
at Myl'em. A smalt oannon which was found in Lyngkyfdam
area was brought to Shillong, and used to be displayed at the
junction of the Kench's Trace road and the national High way
at the Police duty point opposite the General's point near tbe
Garrison ground. Another was a matchlock gun about 5 feet
in length which was used to be kept in the ancestral house of
the descendants of U Bor Manick at Myllem with two
bayonets. Unfortunately the gun was spoiled through
inadvertence end careless use by ignorant persons. Only the
bayonets are still preserved but they will fit only in muzzle
loading guns. The gun at Myiliem used tobe calied 'Ka Man".
How the S8id weapons came tobe in possession of U Bor
Manick there are no records, but it is possible that he obtained
them either from the Ahoms in Astern or captared from the
Moghul descendants of Sylhet, wi h whom the Khasi Syiems
had contacts before the advent of the British.
Thus both U Tlrot Singh of Nongkhlaw and U Bor Manick
of Shillong, did put up heroic fights against the British, as Mr.
V. Bareh has described in his drama. Besides these Syiems,

Other brave men like U Mon Bhut. U Lorshon Jarain, U Khein
Kongor and certain women were depicted in U Tirot Singh"
as fightars who played important parts in resisting the British
Imperialists. Mr. Bareh deserves credit for having brought
these personalities to life through his drama which he has
produced and acted on tha stage on more than one occasions.
U Tirot Singh is ons of the works by recent Khasi writers
which every one should read to appreeiate. From the few
non-Khesis with I had a talk about -'U Tirot Sigh" I could see
that they also like the play whan acted on the stage.
In conclusion I would reiterate that personally regard Tirot
Sigh" as a fine piece of work which deserves help and sncou
ragement frem all and sundry. I would commend it to the reading
public to read and critlcee it to that the drama may further bo
improved if and when the author considers It necesary.
I wish Mr. Victor Bareh every succes in hie future works
and may God grant him health and spirit to produaa mara
writings for tha bsnsfit of tha futura gansratlona.
